newsitem.title: USA: Gold risk higher than volatility implies - CPM.
newsitem.headline: Gold risk higher than volatility implies - CPM.

text.p: The risk of a sharp movement in gold prices is higher than implied by recent historically low volatility in the gold market, CPM Group managing director Jeffrey Christian said Tuesday.
"There is a great deal of risk out there," Christian told analysts attending the New York-based research group's 1996 gold market survey.

"Speculators are more negative on gold now than they have been in all but one previous time period in the past ten years, namely January 1995, according to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Commitment of Traders report," Christian noted.

In the latest CFTC Commitment of Traders report, for the week ended October 22, large non-commercial traders held a record net short position of 36,015 lots in COMEX gold futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Spot gold prices saw their lowest levels since March 1995 last week at $376.70.
"However, just a few months ago, in January 1996, speculators were the most positive they have ever been on gold," Christian said.
In January 1996, speculators held a record net long position of 70,000 lots as the gold price rose to a six year high at $417 an ounce.
"This illustrates how quickly investor sentiments change in the gold market."
But short term implied volatilities in the options market have reached record lows around four percent this year, analysts noted.
"Measured quarterly, gold price volatility topped out at 3.6 pct in the first quarter, dropping to 1.7 pct in the second quarter and 1.3 pct in the third quarter this year," Christian noted.
Investor demand has played the major role in the gold market this year, according to the CPM Group's "Gold Survey 1996".
Investment demand has a weighting of 23 percent in CPM Group's econometric model used to determine the price of gold.
Jewelry demand has the highest weighting at 39 pct, with mine production at 16 pct and central bank activity at 12 pct.

"A surge in investor interest sent gold prices significantly higher in January and February 1996, to $419.30 (basis Comex nearby active contract) on concerns about the sustainability of last year's huge rally in U.S. equity prices," Christian said.
"But when investor demand for gold faded starting in March, prices fell back below $400, down to below $380 last week."
"There are signs investors are taking a fresh look at gold in the fourth quarter 1996, again concerned that U.S. equity markets may be headed for a sharp technical sell off."
Investors are forecast to add about 2.2 million ounces to their net holdings this year, an increase of 47 pct from 1995, the CPM Group's 1996 survey says.
In 1997 net investment demand could reach 3.9 million ounces.
Investors have been net sellers of bullion in 1995 and 1996, although coin and medallion purchases have offset these sales.
--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641.
